title: Story Steps: Read It Twice
child_idea: Read a story twice. Then write one number sentence for each step: add, or take away.

lines.text: @rec

Good morning, inquirers! This is our last lesson of the term. Pencil, paper, your workbook and some counters on the table, please. Today we read stories twice. At the end we do our end-of-term check on your own paper. This lesson is recorded: me and the screen only. You may switch your camera off whenever you like.
Greet each child by first name. Check each camera shows the child and the table, and that the closed check sheet, a ruler and a pencil are ready.
Lesson 10 only: say once that the check is private and not a race. Routine slides and the four inquirer rules are not repeated; they were introduced in Lesson 1.
@rec
I think of a number. Use your fingers or counters to find it. I add 3, and I get 8. What is my number?
I take away 2, and I get 6. What was my number?
I add 10, and I get thirty-five. What was my number?
Story words. Gets, finds and buys mean add. Gives away, eats and loses mean take away.
Siti eats 3 sweets. Add or take away?
Ali finds 5 more shells. Add or take away?
Mei gives away 2 stickers. Add or take away?
4 more children join the line. Add or take away?
Tens and ones, quickly. Think of bundles of ten.
Forty plus twenty?
Thirty-seven plus ten?
Fifty-six take away twenty?
Twenty-four plus five?
Story to number sentence. Ben has 6 cards. He gets 4 more. Which number sentence fits: 6 plus 4, or 6 take away 4?
Which one fits? And what is the answer?
Siti has 9 beads and loses 3. Which sentence, and the answer?
Ali has 12 marbles and wins 5. Which sentence, and the answer?
If a child hesitates on 47 or 36, say the tens word slowly (forty... seven) and point to the bundles: 37 + 10 is one more bundle.

Answers: 5, 8, 25; take away, add, take away, add; 60, 47, 36, 29; then 6 + 4 = 10, 9 - 3 = 6, 12 + 5 = 17. Children answer with fingers, hands or a whispered number. Nobody writes. Joining cold: all you need is counting to 20.
@rec
Two sneak-peek puzzles: ideas we have not learnt yet. A guess is a great start. Nobody is marked.
Puzzle one. Ali has 4 marbles. Ben has 3 more marbles than Ali. How many marbles does Ben have? You may draw them.
Children draw or write the number on their own paper.
Puzzle two. How many marbles do Ali and Ben have altogether? Write the number. Then write what you did first.
Children write or draw their answer.
Everyone holds their paper to the camera at the same moment, once, after puzzle two. Do not read answers aloud. No private chat.
Thank you. We will come back to puzzle two later.

Puzzle 1 answer: 7. Puzzle 2 answer: 11 (first Ben has 4 + 3 = 7, then 4 + 7). Look for good ideas to praise later (a drawing of two groups, or a child who said Ben first). Do not write scores or keep a list.
@rec
Today your counters are the teachers. I read a story twice. You act it out, one step at a time.
Story A. Mei has 8 buttons. She gets 5 more buttons. Then she gives away 6 buttons. How many buttons does Mei have now?
Mei has 8 buttons. She gets 5 more buttons. Then she gives away 6 buttons.
Round 1: children act out story A with counters or the kit squares. Tutor scans the cameras and asks a few children to show their counters.
How many buttons does Mei have now? What did you do first?
Read it twice. First read: who is in the story and what happens? Second read: which numbers, and what is the question?
Story B. Ravi has 12 stickers. He gives 5 stickers to Siti. Then he finds 3 more stickers. How many stickers does Ravi have now?
Round 2: children act out story B with counters, one step at a time.
How many stickers does Ravi have now? Which step came first?
Story C. Ben has 9 balls. Mei has 4 more balls than Ben. How many balls do they have altogether?
Ben has 9 balls. Mei has 4 more balls than Ben.
Round 3: children build Ben's pile, then Mei's pile that is 4 more, then put both together.
How many balls does Mei have? How many do they have altogether?
Mei has more, so Mei has the greater number. Find Mei first. Then put both piles together.
What did you notice? How many steps did each story have? Did each step add or take away?
Each step is one thing: one add or one take away. Step 2 starts from the answer to Step 1.
A child who loses count: put the first number out, then add or remove counters one step at a time and say the new total after each step. A child with too few counters: use the kit squares.

Answers: story A 7 (8 + 5 = 13, then 13 - 6 = 7); story B 10 (12 - 5 = 7, then 7 + 3 = 10); story C: Mei 13, together 22 (9 + 4 = 13, then 9 + 13 = 22). Main room only: no breakout rooms, so you can see every camera. Building with counters is for every child.
@rec
Our trick: read it twice, then one number sentence for each step.
How many number sentences do we write for a story with two steps?

Mei has 26 stickers. Ali gives her 10 more stickers. Then she gives 5 stickers to Ben. Step 1: she gets more, so add. Twenty-six plus ten is thirty-six. Step 2: she gives away, so take away. Thirty-six take away five is thirty-one.
Where did the thirty-six come from?
Your turn. Siti has 40 beads. She uses 20 beads for a bracelet. Then she buys 7 more beads. How many beads does Siti have now? Write Step 1 and Step 2.
Children write two number sentences on their own paper.
Forty take away twenty is twenty. Twenty plus seven is twenty-seven.
More than and fewer than. Ali has 14. Ben has 5 more, so Ben has 19. Ben has 5 fewer, so Ben has 9. Ask: who has more?
Ben has 5 more than Ali, and Ali has 14. Does Ben have more or fewer?
Your turn. Mei has 38 stickers. Siti has 6 fewer stickers than Mei. How many stickers does Siti have? Write the number sentence.
Children write one number sentence on their own paper.
Thirty-eight take away six is thirty-two. Siti has thirty-two stickers.
Who has more, Mei or Siti? How do you know?
A trap! Ravi is in a line. 5 children are in front of Ravi and 2 are behind him. How many children are in the line? Count Ravi too: 5 plus 2 plus 1 is 8.
Children line up counters on the table: 5 in front, one for Ravi, 2 behind. They count every counter.
Who is in the group? Did we count everyone?
If a child reads fewer than as add: ask who has more, and who has the greater number. If a child leaves Ravi out: put counters in a line on camera and touch each one.

Key words to use every time: step, read it twice, more than, fewer than, number sentence. Do not teach bar strips (Lesson 12). Keep every Start here step within 100 and without renaming; the Think harder page has the first renaming.
@rec
Stand up and sip some water. Small steps forward to add, small steps back to take away. Add 3, take away 2, add 4, take away 5. Where do you end up?
Call the four moves. Children step or lean forward and back, in the space they have. Count aloud together. Everyone ends back at the chair.
@rec

Page 1, Start here. Question 1: Ben has 30 cards. He gives 20 cards away. After that, he gets 6 more cards. Fill in the steps. Question 2: Mei has 42 stickers. She gets 7 more stickers. Then she gives 10 stickers to Ali. Write one number sentence for each step. Then write how many stickers Mei has now. Question 3: Ravi has 25 pencils. He buys 10 more pencils. Then he loses 3 pencils. Circle the two number sentences that fit the story.
Page 1, questions 1 to 3. Tutor walks the cameras, asks how do you know. Wait 10 seconds before helping.
Question 1: ten, then sixteen. Question 2: forty-nine, then thirty-nine. Question 3: circle 25 plus 10 and 35 take away 3. Ravi has thirty-two. Mark your own page in another colour.

Page 2. Question 4: write plus or minus in each box. Question 5: Ali has 23 marbles. Ben has 10 more than Ali. How many marbles altogether? Question 6: A bus has 30 children. 10 children get off. Then 4 children get on. Siti writes 30 plus 10 equals 40 for Step 1. Is Siti correct? Circle Yes or No. Then find how many children are on the bus now.
Page 2, questions 4 to 6.

Question 4: plus, minus, minus, plus. Question 5: Ben has thirty-three. They have fifty-six. Question 6: no. Children who get off leave the bus, so take away. Thirty take away ten is twenty. Twenty plus four is twenty-four.
When you have finished Start here, you can choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation. Everyone may choose. You can take pages 3 to 5 home.
Choice time: Think harder (page 3), Go further (page 4), the Investigation (page 5), or finish and check your own work. Tutor never says who is on which page.

Q1: say what happens first; gives away means take away. Q2: use counters, one step at a time. Q3: ask which sentence starts from the answer of the first. Q4: does the word make it greater or smaller? Q5: find Ben first. Q6: ask who leaves the bus.
Think harder T1: Ravi has more, so Mei has fewer; draw two groups. T2: draw the line and touch each child, Mei too. T3: find Mei first, then Siti. Go further: write one step at a time.

A child who is still stuck ticks 'I am still stuck' on the look-back page. You check in during the open session at the start of Term 2 (a quick visit to the shared room or a hand signal, parent nearby). Never a private message.

Think harder is for ideas taught today in a new setting (reversed wording, the group trap). Go further is mastery and extension. Do not announce who is on which page. Pairs are never split unless both children agree. Start here pages 1 and 2 are the target; the rest of the workbook time is for choosing, and pages 3 to 5 may go home.
@rec
Siti has 20 stickers. Ali has 5 fewer stickers than Siti. Ravi says Ali has 25 stickers. Do you agree? Use counters to explain.
Build 20 and take 5 away with your counters. Is Ravi right?
Talk to the grown-up next to you or to your screen for one minute. Use the sentence starter: I think... because...
Who would like to share? Volunteers first. A pass is always fine.
Remember puzzle two? Ben has 3 more than Ali, and Ali has 4. Ben has seven. Together they have eleven.
Did anyone change their mind about puzzle two while we worked? You can just nod.
Model answer: No. Fewer means less. Ali has 20 - 5 = 15. Volunteers first; never call a child by name to answer; no tallies, no rankings. Praise the reason, not the speed.
@rec
Exit ticket. Three questions, on your own, without looking back. Write your answers on page 5.
Children answer E1 to E3 on their own.
Everyone holds their ticket to the camera at the same moment so only you see it. No private chat.
Eighteen. Eleven. Thirteen.
Check your own ticket in a different colour. Well done. Now we put the workbook away for the check.

The end-of-term check. Ten questions, one from each lesson, and one optional Think harder question. It takes about twenty minutes, on your own paper. It is not a race. You may skip any question. I will not say any answers, and I will not show anyone's paper.
Children take out the closed check sheet, a pencil and a ruler. Grown-ups sit nearby and do not give answers. Paper flat on the table, not held up. Name on page 1.

Page 1. Question 1. Look at the sticks. How many bundles of ten, and how many single sticks? Write them. Then write how many sticks there are altogether. Question 2. Fill in the blanks. Part a: look at the number line. Which number is the arrow pointing to? Part b: write fifty-three in digits.
Children work quietly on page 1 (questions 1 and 2). Walk the cameras; say nothing about right or wrong. If asked, re-read a question to the whole group.
Turn to page 2.

Question 3. You have two cards, 3 and 8. Use both cards to make two different numbers. Write them. Then write the greater number. Question 4. Fill in the missing numbers. Part a: count on in fives and write the next two numbers. Part b: count on in tens and write the next two numbers. Question 5. Look at the ten frames: 7 and 5. Write 7 plus 5. Then write 37 plus 5.
Children work quietly on page 2 (questions 3 to 5).
One-minute stretch: stand, shake out your hands, sip some water. Paper stays on the table.
Turn to page 3. You need your ruler for question 9.

Question 6. Part a: write 52 plus 30. Part b: write 52 take away 20. Question 7. Write 74 take away 31. Question 8. Fill in the missing number in each box. Part a: 8 plus 4 equals 6 plus box. Part b: 60 plus 10 equals 50 plus box. Question 9. Use your ruler. Part a: draw a line 6 centimetres long, starting at the dot. Part b: write how long a line 4 centimetres longer than your line is.
Children work quietly on page 3 (questions 6 to 9).
Turn to page 4.

Question 10. Read it twice. Mei has 35 stickers. Ali gives her 10 more stickers. Then she gives 3 stickers to Ben. Write a number sentence for Step 1 and for Step 2. Then write how many stickers Mei has now. The last question is a Think harder question, and it is optional. You may skip it. Ali is in a line. There are 5 children in front of him and 3 children behind him. How many children are in the line?
Children work quietly on page 4: question 10, then the optional Think harder question if they wish.

Pencils down. Check that your name is on page 1 and close your sheet. Well done for trying your best. Grown-ups, please take one photo of each page today and send them to the business WhatsApp, as in the note. I will send a short note about your learning, never a mark.
Say nothing about answers. Remind the group that no score is shown and no answer is read out. Children who did not finish may use the flex time at the end.

A child who says they cannot do a question: say to the whole group that skipping is fine and they may come back. A child who is upset: the grown-up may stop at any time; do not single the child out. Never give a hint to one child about an answer.

Exit ticket tracker (tutor only): S = secure on all three, D = developing (one wrong), H = needs another go (two or three wrong). Never read out a child's result. This is not the end-of-term check.

Children fill in the look-back box on page 5.

Optional, only if you are on time: Ali has 20 marbles. He wins 6 and loses 4. Does it matter which comes first?
Short think time, then take two answers.

slides.title: Story Steps

blocks.head: TODAY WE WILL
items: Read stories twice and write one step at a time.
Then we show what we learned this term.

slides.note: Lesson 10 of Term 1, the last lesson of the term. 90 minutes. Objective: read a short story twice and write one number sentence for each step. Time plan: opening 0 to 2, warm-up 2 to 8, sneak-peek 8 to 12, explore 12 to 22, mini-lesson 22 to 32, brain break 32 to 35, workbook 35 to 55, talk 55 to 59, exit ticket and end-of-term check 59 to 83, look-back 83 to 85, flex time and goodbye 85 to 90 (the buffer: do not start anything new). Think harder, Go further and the Investigation are for every child to choose. Nobody is told which page they should be on. Tell the group the lesson is recorded (you and the screen only) and that a child may keep the camera off. Say that the check at the end is on private paper and is not a race.
slides.subtitle: Read it twice: addition and subtraction in stories

mascot.say: Hi, I'm Mi. Let's notice, test and explain why!

slides.title: Warm-up: I think of a number

blocks.text: Use your fingers or counters

cols.text: I think of a number. I add 3. I get 8.

slides.note: Say: I think of a number, I add 3, I get 8. Children use fingers or counters to find the number: 5 (8 take away 3). Then: I think of a number, I take away 2, I get 6 (answer 8). Then: I think of a number, I add 10, I get 35 (answer 25). This is the holiday-course game I think of a number, used only as a warm-up; no writing.

slides.title: Story words

rows: gives away, eats, loses, leaves, how many left

blocks.text: Add or take away? Say it.

slides.note: Read the two rows aloud, then ask: Siti eats 3 sweets (take away). Ali finds 5 more shells (add). Mei gives away 2 stickers (take away). 4 more children join (add). Children answer aloud or with a thumb up for add and down for take away. Say that today we also meet the words more than and fewer than.

slides.title: Tens and ones, quickly

blocks.text: Say the answers. Think of tens and ones.

slides.note: Answers: 60, 47, 36, 29. Show 37 as 3 bundles and 7 singles: 37 + 10 is one more bundle, 47. 56 - 20 takes 2 bundles, 36. 24 + 5 adds 5 singles, 29. This is spiral review of adding and taking away tens and ones, so a child who joins cold can do the lesson. Say the tens word slowly: forty-seven.

slides.title: Story to number sentence

blocks.text: Ben has 6 cards. He gets 4 more.
Which one fits the story?

slides.note: Read each short story twice and ask which number sentence fits, then the answer. Ben has 6 cards and gets 4 more: 6 + 4 = 10. Siti has 9 beads and loses 3: 9 - 3 = 6. Ali has 12 marbles and wins 5: 12 + 5 = 17. Children answer aloud or show a thumb up for the first sentence and down for the second. No writing yet.

slides.title: Sneak-peek puzzles

blocks.text: Ideas we have not learnt yet. A guess is a great start. Nobody is marked.

cols.head: PUZZLE 1: anyone can try
items: Ali has 4 marbles.
Ben has 3 more marbles than Ali.
How many marbles does Ben have?
You may draw them.

cols.head: PUZZLE 2: think
items: How many marbles do Ali and Ben have altogether?
Write the number. Then write what you did first.

slides.note: Puzzle 1 is an access question: any child can draw 4 marbles and 3 more, and count. Puzzle 2 is the thinking question on the key idea (two steps). Say: two sneak-peek puzzles, ideas we have not learnt yet; a guess is a great start and I do not know is welcome; nobody is marked. Children write on their own paper and everyone holds the paper to the camera once, at the same moment, after puzzle 2. Do not read answers aloud. Puzzle 1 answer 7; puzzle 2 answer 11, first Ben has 4 + 3 = 7.

slides.title: Explore: act it out

items: Listen once. Picture the story.
Listen again. Put out counters for the first number.
Do each step with your counters.
Say: how many now?

blocks.head: STORY A
items: Mei has 8 buttons. She gets 5 more buttons. Then she gives away 6 buttons.

slides.note: Round 1, about 3 minutes, objects first and no writing. Read story A twice: Mei has 8 buttons. She gets 5 more buttons. Then she gives away 6 buttons. How many buttons does Mei have now? Children act it out with counters or the kit squares: 8 and 5 more is 13, then 6 away leaves 7. Ask a few children to show their counters to the camera. Answer for the tutor: 7.

slides.title: Read it twice

cols.head: FIRST READ
items: Who is in the story?
What happens?
No numbers yet.

cols.head: SECOND READ
items: Which numbers?
What is the question?
One step at a time.

blocks.head: STORY B
items: Ravi has 12 stickers. He gives 5 stickers to Siti. Then he finds 3 more stickers.

slides.note: Round 2, about 3 minutes. Read story B twice, with a first read for who and what, then a second read for the numbers and the question: Ravi has 12 stickers. He gives 5 stickers to Siti. Then he finds 3 more stickers. How many stickers does Ravi have now? Children act it out: 12 - 5 = 7, then 7 + 3 = 10. Answer for the tutor: 10. Praise the two reads, not the speed.

slides.title: Who has more?

blocks.head: STORY C
items: Ben has 9 balls. Mei has 4 more balls than Ben.
How many balls do they have altogether?

blocks.text: Find Mei first. Then put them together.

slides.note: Round 3, about 3 minutes. Read story C twice: Ben has 9 balls. Mei has 4 more balls than Ben. How many balls do they have altogether? Children act it out with counters: a pile of 9 for Ben, then a pile for Mei that is 4 more (13), then put both piles together (22). Answer for the tutor: Mei 13, together 22. Say that Mei has more, so her pile is the greater one. This sets up question 5 in the workbook.

slides.title: What did we notice?

items: How many steps did each story have?
Did each step add, or take away?
Where did Step 2 start?

slides.note: Take one or two answers from volunteers. Key ideas: each story had two steps; each step was one add or one take away; Step 2 starts from the answer to Step 1. Repeat a child's answer in your own words so the recording picks it up. This sets up the mini-lesson.

slides.title: Read it twice, then step by step

cols.head: FIRST READ
items: Who? What happens?

cols.head: SECOND READ
items: Which numbers? What is asked?

blocks.text: One step, one number sentence

slides.note: Name the routine: read it twice, then write one number sentence for each step. First read: who and what, no numbers. Second read: the numbers and the question. Then each step is one add or one take away. Ask: how many number sentences for a two-step story? Answer: two.

slides.title: Mei's stickers

blocks.head: STORY
items: Mei has 26 stickers. Ali gives her 10 more stickers. Then she gives 5 stickers to Ben. How many stickers does Mei have now?

slides.note: Think aloud. First read: Mei, stickers, Ali gives, she gives to Ben. Second read: 26, 10 more, 5 to Ben. Step 1: gets more, so add, 26 + 10 = 36 (one more bundle of ten). Step 2: gives away, so take away, 36 - 5 = 31 (no renaming: 6 - 5 = 1). Write the answer in a sentence. Ask: where did 36 come from? Answer: from Step 1.

slides.title: Your turn: two steps

blocks.text: Write Step 1 and Step 2 on your paper. About 1 minute.

blocks.head: STORY
items: Siti has 40 beads. She uses 20 beads for a bracelet. Then she buys 7 more beads. How many beads does Siti have now?

slides.note: Read the story twice. Each child writes on their own paper; walk the cameras. Do not ask children to hold boards up in front of the group. Answer for the tutor: 40 - 20 = 20, then 20 + 7 = 27.

slides.title: Check: two steps

blocks.text: Siti has 27 beads.

slides.note: Answers: 40 - 20 = 20 and 20 + 7 = 27. Read each answer aloud so a child watching the recording can mark their own work. Ask: which words told us to take away? (uses) And to add? (buys more).

start.text: Ben has 30 cards. He gives 20 cards away. After that, he gets 6 more cards.
start.hint: Say what happens first. Gives away means take away. Gets more means add.
start.solution: First, Ben gives away 20, so we take away: 30 - 20 = 10. Then he gets 6 more, so we add: 10 + 6 = 16. Ben has 16 cards now.
mistakes: Adding the 20 (30 + 20) because 20 is in the story.
Using 30 again in Step 2 instead of the 10 left after Step 1.

start.text: Mei has 42 stickers. She gets 7 more stickers. Then she gives 10 stickers to Ali. Write one number sentence for each step.
start.hint: Use counters or draw it. What happens first? Then what happens next?
start.solution: Step 1: she gets 7 more, so add: 42 + 7 = 49. Step 2: she gives 10 away, so take away: 49 - 10 = 39. Mei has 39 stickers now.

start.text: Ravi has 25 pencils. He buys 10 more pencils. Then he loses 3 pencils. Circle the 2 number sentences that fit the story.
start.hint: Buys more means add. Loses means take away. The second step starts from the answer to the first.
start.solution: Step 1: buys 10 more, so 25 + 10 = 35. Step 2: loses 3, so 35 - 3 = 32. The sentences 25 - 10 = 15 and 35 + 3 = 38 use the wrong sign.
mistakes: Circling 25 - 3 = 22 because both numbers are in the story.
Circling a sentence with the wrong sign.

parts.text: Ali has 8 shells. He finds 5 more shells. 8 [] 5 = 13
Siti has 9 sweets. She eats 3 sweets. 9 [] 3 = 6
Mei has 10 stickers. She gives away 4 stickers. 10 [] 4 = 6
There are 12 children in a line. 6 more children join the line. 12 [] 6 = 18

start.hint: Does the story word make the number greater or smaller? Gets more makes it greater.
start.solution: Finds more means add (+). Eats means take away (-). Gives away means take away (-). Join means more, so add (+).
mistakes: Choosing + for gives away because there is a number in the sentence.

start.text: Ali has 23 marbles. Ben has 10 more than Ali. How many marbles do they have altogether? Use counters if you like.
start.answer: Step 1: Ben has 23 + 10 = 33. Step 2: 23 + 33 = 56. They have 56 marbles.
start.hint: Read it twice. First find how many Ben has. Then put Ali and Ben together.
start.solution: Step 1: Ben has 10 more than Ali, so 23 + 10 = 33. Step 2: altogether means add Ali and Ben: 23 + 33 = 56 marbles.

start.text: A bus has 30 children. 10 children get off. Then 4 children get on. Siti writes 30 + 10 = 40 for Step 1.

parts.text: Is Siti right? Circle Yes or No.

start.answer: No. Get off means take away: 30 - 10 = 20. Then 20 + 4 = 24. There are 24 children.
start.hint: Who leaves the bus? Do they make the bus fuller or emptier?
start.solution: Children who get off leave the bus, so Step 1 is a take away: 30 - 10 = 20. Siti added the 10. Then 4 get on, so add: 20 + 4 = 24.

think.text: Ravi has 15 marbles. He has 3 more marbles than Mei.
think.answer: Mei has 12 marbles. Together they have 27.
think.hint: Ravi has more, so Mei has fewer. Draw two groups of counters and compare them.
think.solution: Ravi has 3 more than Mei, so Mei has 3 fewer than Ravi: 15 - 3 = 12. Together: 15 + 12 = 27 marbles.
mistakes: Adding 15 + 3 = 18 because the word more is there.

think.text: Mei is in a line to buy lunch. There are 6 children in front of her and 4 children behind her. How many children are in the line?

parts.text: There are ___ children in the line.

think.hint: Draw the line of children. Did you draw Mei too?
think.solution: The children in front are 6 and behind are 4: 6 + 4 = 10. Mei is in the line as well, so 10 + 1 = 11 children.

think.text: Ben has 12 marbles. Mei has 5 more marbles than Ben. Siti has 3 fewer marbles than Mei. How many marbles does Siti have?
think.hint: Find Mei first. Then Siti has fewer than Mei.
think.solution: Step 1: Mei has 5 more than Ben: 12 + 5 = 17. Step 2: Siti has 3 fewer than Mei: 17 - 3 = 14 marbles.
mistakes: Taking 3 from 12 (Siti is compared with Mei, not Ben).

go.text: A shop has 60 pencils. It sells 24 pencils on Monday and 15 pencils on Tuesday. On Wednesday, a box of 30 pencils comes in. Write one number sentence for each step.
go.answer: Step 1: 60 - 24 = 36. Step 2: 36 - 15 = 21. Step 3: 21 + 30 = 51. The shop has 51 pencils.
go.hint: There are three things that happen, so there are three steps. Write one number sentence for each.
go.solution: Monday: 60 - 24 = 36. Tuesday: 36 - 15 = 21. Wednesday a box comes in, so add: 21 + 30 = 51 pencils.
mistakes: Adding 24 and 15 and taking that from 60 but forgetting the box.

go.text: Step 1: 25 + 10 = 35. Step 2: 35 - 8 = 27. Write a story that fits both steps. End your story with a question. Many stories are right.
go.answer: Any story where 25 grows by 10 and then 8 are taken away, and the question asks how many now. The answer is 27.
go.hint: Pick who and what. Step 1 adds 10. Step 2 takes away 8. What could 25 be?
go.solution: For example: Ali has 25 stickers. He gets 10 more. Then he gives 8 to his sister. How many stickers does Ali have now? 25 + 10 = 35, 35 - 8 = 27.
mistakes: A story where the second step starts from 25 instead of 35.

go.text: Mei, Ali and Ben have 70 shells altogether. Mei has 25 shells. Ali has 10 more shells than Mei. Write one number sentence for each step. How many shells does Ben have?
go.answer: Ali has 35. Mei and Ali have 60. Ben has 10 shells.
go.hint: Find Ali first. Then find how many Mei and Ali have together.
go.solution: Step 1: Ali has 25 + 10 = 35. Step 2: Mei and Ali have 25 + 35 = 60. Step 3: Ben has the rest: 70 - 60 = 10 shells.

investigation.title: Does the order matter?
investigation.first: Start at 20. Add 10, then take away 5. Start again at 20. Take away 5 first, then add 10. Is the answer the same?
investigation.text: Pick your own numbers. Try both orders. Is the answer always the same? When can one order not work?
investigation.answer: Both orders give the same answer (20 + 10 - 5 = 25 and 20 - 5 + 10 = 25) whenever both orders can be done. But the order can matter for what you are allowed to do: from 4 you cannot take away 6 first, though 4 + 10 - 6 = 8 works. So: the answer is the same, but you cannot take away more than you have.
val: same answer when both orders can be done
cannot take away more than you have
investigation.look_for: A child who tests several numbers, says what they notice, and finds a case where taking away first is not possible (start 4, take away 6).
mistakes: Testing only one example and saying always.
Thinking the answer changes because the numbers change places.

talk.question: Siti has 20 stickers. Ali has 5 fewer stickers than Siti. Ravi says Ali has 25 stickers. Do you agree? Use counters to explain.
talk.answer: No. Fewer means less. Ali has 5 fewer than 20, so Ali has 20 - 5 = 15 stickers. Siti has more than Ali, so 25 cannot be right.
talk.look_for: A reason that uses the word fewer or less and shows 20 with 5 taken away (not just because 25 is too big).

exit.text: A bus has 25 children. 10 children get off. Then 3 children get on. How many children are on the bus now?
exit.solution: Get off means take away: 25 - 10 = 15. Get on means add: 15 + 3 = 18.

exit.text: Ben has 6 stickers. Mei has 5 more stickers than Ben. How many stickers does Mei have?
exit.solution: Mei has more than Ben, so add: 6 + 5 = 11.

exit.text: Siti has 20 beads. Ali has 7 fewer beads than Siti. How many beads does Ali have?
exit.solution: Ali has fewer, so take away: 20 - 7 = 13.
mistakes: Writing 27 (adding because the number 7 is there).

menu.title: Is it always true?
menu.tutor: Mei says: you can add and take away in any order and get the same answer. Is that always true? Try 20 + 10 - 5, then 20 - 5 + 10, then 4 - 6 + 10.
menu.rec: Recording: pause. Try 20 + 10 - 5 and 20 - 5 + 10. Then try 4 - 6 first. What do you notice?
menu.answer: 20 + 10 - 5 = 25 and 20 - 5 + 10 = 25: the same. But from 4 you cannot take away 6 first. The answer is the same when both orders can be done.

menu.title: Make a story puzzle
menu.tutor: Write a two-step story for your grown-up with numbers within 100. Write the question. Keep your own answer secret, then check theirs.
menu.rec: Recording: pause. Write a two-step story and a question for your grown-up to solve.
menu.answer: No single answer. Check that each step is one add or one take away and the question matches.

menu.title: Teach it back
menu.tutor: Pretend a toy has never heard of reading a story twice. Teach it using: Ali has 20 marbles, wins 6 and loses 4.
menu.rec: Recording: pause. Teach a toy or a grown-up to read a story twice. Use 20, win 6, lose 4.
menu.answer: First read: who and what. Second read: the numbers and the question. Step 1: 20 + 6 = 26. Step 2: 26 - 4 = 22.

questions.skill: Tens and ones: read a picture of sticks in tens and ones
questions.text: Count the sticks. Fill in the blanks.
questions.say: Question 1. Look at the sticks. How many bundles of ten, and how many single sticks? Write them. Then write how many sticks there are altogether.
questions.solution: 3 bundles of ten is 30, and 9 singles makes 39.
questions.partly: Two of the three correct (for example 39 but the tens and ones swapped).
mistakes: Counting each bundle as one stick (3 + 9 = 12).

questions.skill: Number line to 100 (the number the arrow shows) and a number word in digits

parts.text: Look at the number line. The arrow is pointing to ___.

questions.say: Question 2. Fill in the blanks. Part a: look at the number line. Which number is the arrow pointing to? Part b: write fifty-three in digits.
questions.solution: The arrow is just after 66 and just before 68, so it points to 67. Fifty-three is 5 tens and 3 ones: 53.

questions.skill: Make two numbers from two cards and say which is greater
questions.text: Look at the two cards. Use both cards to make 2 different numbers.
questions.say: Question 3. You have two cards, 3 and 8. Use both cards to make two different numbers. Write them. Then write the greater number.
questions.solution: Put 3 first and 8 second to make 38. Put 8 first and 3 second to make 83. 83 has 8 tens and 38 has 3 tens, so 83 is greater.
questions.right: 38 and 83 (either order) and 83 as the greater.
questions.partly: Both numbers made but the greater one wrong, or only one number made and the greater one right.
mistakes: Saying 38 is greater because 8 is the greater digit.

questions.say: Question 4. Fill in the missing numbers. Part a: count on in fives and write the next two numbers. Part b: count on in tens and write the next two numbers.
questions.solution: In 5s: 50, 55, 60. In 10s: 34, 44, 54 (the tens digit goes up by 1 and the ones digit stays 4).
questions.partly: Two or three of the four gaps correct.

questions.skill: Add by making a ten, then with a tens number
questions.text: Look at the ten frames. Fill in the missing numbers.
questions.say: Question 5. Look at the ten frames: 7 and 5. Write 7 plus 5. Then write 37 plus 5.
questions.solution: 7 + 3 = 10, and 2 more makes 12. 37 + 3 = 40, and 2 more makes 42.
mistakes: (b) 32 or 312 (joining digits or forgetting the tens).

questions.skill: Add and take away tens (jumps of ten)
questions.say: Question 6. Part a: write 52 plus 30. Part b: write 52 take away 20.
questions.solution: 3 tens more than 52 is 82. 2 tens fewer is 32. The ones digit stays 2.

questions.skill: Take away tens and ones without renaming
questions.solution: 74 - 30 = 44, then 44 - 1 = 43. Or 7 tens and 4 ones take away 3 tens and 1 one leaves 4 tens and 3 ones.
questions.partly: The tens digit right or the ones digit right, but not both (for example 44 or 33).

questions.skill: Equals as a balance: a box number
questions.say: Question 8. Fill in the missing number in each box. Part a: 8 plus 4 equals 6 plus box. Part b: 60 plus 10 equals 50 plus box.
questions.solution: (a) 8 + 4 = 12, and 12 is 6 + 6, so the box is 6. (b) 60 + 10 = 70, and 70 is 50 + 20, so the box is 20. Both sides must have the same total.
mistakes: (a) 12 (writing the total of the left side).
(b) 70 (the total instead of the missing number).

questions.skill: Draw a line of a given length, then find a length 4 cm longer

parts.text: Draw a line 6 cm long. Start at the dot.
parts.ans: A line from the dot, 6 cm long (5.7 to 6.3 cm)

parts.text: A line 4 cm longer than your line is ___ cm long.

questions.say: Question 9. Use your ruler. Part a: draw a line 6 centimetres long, starting at the dot. Part b: write how long a line 4 centimetres longer than your line is.
questions.solution: Put the 0 mark of the ruler on the dot and draw to the 6 mark. A line 4 cm longer is 6 + 4 = 10 cm.
questions.right: The line is about right (5.7 to 6.3 cm) and 10 is written.
questions.partly: Only the line about right, or only the 10 written (a line within 0.5 cm of 6 cm counts if the photo is not clear).
mistakes: Starting the line at 1 on the ruler (a 5 cm line).

questions.skill: A two-step story, one operation per step
questions.text: Mei has 35 stickers. Ali gives her 10 more stickers. Then she gives 3 stickers to Ben. Write one number sentence for each step.
questions.say: Question 10. Read it twice. Mei has 35 stickers. Ali gives her 10 more stickers. Then she gives 3 stickers to Ben. Write a number sentence for Step 1 and for Step 2. Then write how many stickers Mei has now.
questions.solution: Step 1: she gets 10 more, so add: 35 + 10 = 45. Step 2: she gives 3 away, so take away: 45 - 3 = 42.
questions.right: Both step sentences have the right operation and numbers (any clear layout) and the answer is 42.
questions.partly: The answer 42 without steps, or one correct step sentence, or both sentences right with one slip in the arithmetic.
mistakes: 32 (taking the 10 away from 35 and adding 3 or similar).

optional.skill: Reading trap: who is in the group
optional.text: Think harder (optional). Ali is in a line. There are 5 children in front of him and 3 children behind him. How many children are in the line?

parts.text: There are ___ children in the line.

optional.say: The last question is a Think harder question, and it is optional. You may skip it. Ali is in a line. There are 5 children in front of him and 3 children behind him. How many children are in the line?
optional.solution: 5 in front and 3 behind makes 8, and Ali is in the line as well: 8 + 1 = 9.
optional.note: Never scored. Whether the child tried it (right or wrong) adds one neutral line to the note; a skipped item adds nothing.
